items.readable_text:
Content:
An important class of improper integrals concerns those involving arctangent.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's consider the following improper integral:

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle{\int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x}]

Content:
First, we recall that

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \arctan(x) + C.]

Content:
So, to evaluate our improper integral, we follow the usual procedure:

Content:
- First, we set the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a.]
- Then, we integrate as usual.
- Finally, we take the limit as [MATH: a \to \infty.]

Content:
So, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{∞}(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (x)]_{0}^{a}; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a) − \arctan (0)]; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a)].]

Content:
Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y = \arctan{x},] shown in the graph below:

Content:
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \big[ \arctan(x) \big] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \big[ \arctan(x) \big] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/575e40049d40450fc0a189fd198c429d]

Content:
Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

items.title: Evaluating an Improper Integral by Applying the Basic Result

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the following result: [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \arctan(x) + C]

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a \to -\infty.] [MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}(4)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx; = 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (x)]_{a}^{0}; = 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (0) − \arctan (a)]; = 4 ⋅ (0 − lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]); = − 4lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y = \arctan{x},] shown in the graph below:

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that [MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}(4)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= − 4lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]; = − 4(− (π)/(2)); = 2π.]

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac{4}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the following result:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \arctan(x) + C]

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a \to -\infty.]
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}(4)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx; = 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (x)]_{a}^{0}; = 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (0) − \arctan (a)]; = 4 ⋅ (0 − lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]); = − 4lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y = \arctan{x},] shown in the graph below:

- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

[IMG: /graphics/6c01ba2881dcb5e3c67965f2a0924e63]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}(4)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= − 4lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]; = − 4(− (π)/(2)); = 2π.]

Content:
We can evaluate more complex integrals involving arctangent by making use of the following results:

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(1 + (kx)^{2})dx|= (1)/(k)\arctan (kx) + C; ∫(1)/(k^{2} + x^{2})dx|= (1)/(k)\arctan ((x)/(k)) + C]

Content:
Let's see some examples.

items.title: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the First Result

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the following result:

[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+(kx)^2} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \arctan \left(kx \right) + C]

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{− 1/4}^{∞}(2)/(1 + 16x^{2})dx|= 2 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{− 1/4}^{a}(1)/(1 + 16x^{2})dx; = 2 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{− 1/4}^{a}(1)/(1 + (4x)^{2})dx; = 2 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[(1)/(4)\arctan (4x)]_{− 1/4}^{a}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)(\arctan (4a) − \arctan (− 1)); = (1)/(2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (4a)] − (− (π)/(4))); = (1)/(2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (4a)] + (π)/(4))]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\arctan{(4x)},] shown in the graph below:

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan{(4x)}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan{(4x)}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{− 1/4}^{∞}(2)/(1 + 16x^{2})dx|= (1)/(2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (4a)] + (π)/(4)); = (1)/(2) ⋅ ((π)/(2) + (π)/(4)); = (3π)/(8).]

items.title: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the Second Result

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the following result:

[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{k^2 + x^2} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \arctan \left( \dfrac{x}{k} \right) + C]

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{∞}(6)/(x^{2} + 4)dx|= 6 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{a}(1)/(x^{2} + 4)dx; = 6 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{a}(1)/(x^{2} + 2^{2})dx; = 6 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[(1)/(2)\arctan ((x)/(2))]_{2sqrt(3)}^{a}; = 3lim_(a → ∞)(\arctan ((a)/(2)) − \arctan (sqrt(3))); = 3lim_(a → ∞)(\arctan ((a)/(2)) − (π)/(3)); = 3lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan ((a)/(2))] − π]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right),] shown in the graph below:

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{∞}(6)/(x^{2} + 4)dx|= 3lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan ((a)/(2))] − π; = 3 ⋅ (π)/(2) − π; = (π)/(2).]

sections.readable_text: Use the substitution [MATH: u = x^2] to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle{\int}_{1}^{\infty} \dfrac{2x}{1 + x^4} \,\textrm{d}x.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we substitute [MATH: u = x^2.] Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =2x \, \textrm{d}x.]

Since [MATH: u \to \infty] when [MATH: x \to \infty,] the table for the limits of integration using the rule [MATH: u = x^2] is as follows:

[MATH: x]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: \infty]

[MATH: u]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: \infty]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable [MATH: u] is [MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}(2x)/(1 + x^{4})dx|= ∫_{1}^{∞}(1)/(1 + u^{2})du.]

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.] [MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}(2x)/(1 + x^{4})dx|= ∫_{1}^{∞}(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{1}^{a}(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (u)]_{1}^{a}; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a) − \arctan (1)]; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a)] − (π)/(4)]

Finally, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\arctan(x),] shown in the graph below:

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[ \arctan(x) \right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[ \arctan(x) \right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that [MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}(2x)/(1 + x^{4})dx|= lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a)] − (π)/(4); = (π)/(2) − (π)/(4); = (π)/(4).]

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \infty] |

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}(2x)/(1 + x^{4})dx|= ∫_{1}^{∞}(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = lim_(a → ∞)∫_{1}^{a}(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (u)]_{1}^{a}; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a) − \arctan (1)]; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a)] − (π)/(4)]

Finally, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\arctan(x),] shown in the graph below:

- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[ \arctan(x) \right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[ \arctan(x) \right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
An important class of improper integrals concerns those involving arctangent.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's consider the following improper integral:

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle{\int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x}]

Content:
First, we recall that

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \arctan(x) + C.]

Content:
So, to evaluate our improper integral, we follow the usual procedure:

Content:
- First, we set the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a.]
- Then, we integrate as usual.
- Finally, we take the limit as [MATH: a \to \infty.]

Content:
So, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{∞}(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= lim_(a → ∞)∫_{0}^{a}(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (x)]_{0}^{a}; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a) − \arctan (0)]; = lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (a)].]

Content:
Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y = \arctan{x},] shown in the graph below:

Content:
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \big[ \arctan(x) \big] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \big[ \arctan(x) \big] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/575e40049d40450fc0a189fd198c429d]

Content:
Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating an Improper Integral by Applying the Basic Result

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac{4}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the following result:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \arctan(x) + C]

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a \to -\infty.]
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}(4)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx; = 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (x)]_{a}^{0}; = 4 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (0) − \arctan (a)]; = 4 ⋅ (0 − lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]); = − 4lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y = \arctan{x},] shown in the graph below:

- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan{x}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

[IMG: /graphics/6c01ba2881dcb5e3c67965f2a0924e63]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}(4)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= − 4lim_(a → − ∞)[\arctan (a)]; = − 4(− (π)/(2)); = 2π.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: A Reminder of Some Useful Results

Content:
We can evaluate more complex integrals involving arctangent by making use of the following results:

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(1 + (kx)^{2})dx|= (1)/(k)\arctan (kx) + C; ∫(1)/(k^{2} + x^{2})dx|= (1)/(k)\arctan ((x)/(k)) + C]

Content:
Let's see some examples.

---

Item 6 — Example: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the First Result

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1/4}^\infty \dfrac {2}{1+16x^2} \,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the following result:

[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+(kx)^2} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \arctan \left(kx \right) + C]

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{− 1/4}^{∞}(2)/(1 + 16x^{2})dx|= 2 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{− 1/4}^{a}(1)/(1 + 16x^{2})dx; = 2 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{− 1/4}^{a}(1)/(1 + (4x)^{2})dx; = 2 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[(1)/(4)\arctan (4x)]_{− 1/4}^{a}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)(\arctan (4a) − \arctan (− 1)); = (1)/(2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (4a)] − (− (π)/(4))); = (1)/(2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (4a)] + (π)/(4))]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\arctan{(4x)},] shown in the graph below:

- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan{(4x)}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan{(4x)}\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

[IMG: /graphics/6f825ead10f726d4996ce7df4d607c5f]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{− 1/4}^{∞}(2)/(1 + 16x^{2})dx|= (1)/(2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan (4a)] + (π)/(4)); = (1)/(2) ⋅ ((π)/(2) + (π)/(4)); = (3π)/(8).]

Item 9 — Example: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the Second Result

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{2\sqrt{3}}^\infty \dfrac{6}{x^2+4} \,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the following result:

[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{k^2 + x^2} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \arctan \left( \dfrac{x}{k} \right) + C]

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{∞}(6)/(x^{2} + 4)dx|= 6 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{a}(1)/(x^{2} + 4)dx; = 6 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{a}(1)/(x^{2} + 2^{2})dx; = 6 ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[(1)/(2)\arctan ((x)/(2))]_{2sqrt(3)}^{a}; = 3lim_(a → ∞)(\arctan ((a)/(2)) − \arctan (sqrt(3))); = 3lim_(a → ∞)(\arctan ((a)/(2)) − (π)/(3)); = 3lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan ((a)/(2))] − π]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right),] shown in the graph below:

- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

[IMG: /graphics/cb07856ca51f2e4c4c57cae7ba76729b]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{2sqrt(3)}^{∞}(6)/(x^{2} + 4)dx|= 3lim_(a → ∞)[\arctan ((a)/(2))] − π; = 3 ⋅ (π)/(2) − π; = (π)/(2).]
